title: VIX Jumped 11.57 Points in a Day; History Says Six Months Later Stocks Were Usually Higher
excerpt: The fear gauge closed at 28.18 on November 5 as the S&P 500 fell 4.41% and the Nasdaq 100 dropped 6.5%. In Bespoke's 19 similar spikes since 1990, the S&P 500's median return six months later was 4.8%, positive 79% of the time — with a negative average over the first month.
body:
• The Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) surged 11.57 points to 28.18 on November 5, 2026, its largest single-day move since the April 2025 tariff week, according to Bespoke Investment Group.
  • The selloff that drove it: the S&P 500 fell 4.41%, the Nasdaq 100 dropped 6.5%, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index sank more than 11% as investors priced in tighter AI regulation after the Democratic midterm sweep.
  • Bespoke's history of 19 similar spikes since 1990: median S&P 500 return of 4.2% at three months (positive 68% of the time) and 4.8% at six months (positive 79%) — but the average one-month return was negative 0.4%.
  • For long-term investors, the sourced takeaway is narrow: past spikes of this kind usually faded, the sample is only 19 events, and February 2020 shows a spike can also precede a much larger fall.

Wall Street's fear gauge had its sharpest one-day move in about a year and a half on Thursday, November 5. The VIX closed at 28.18, up 11.57 points from 16.61 the day before, according to Bespoke Investment Group data reported by BigGo Finance. The VIX uses S&P 500 option prices to measure how much volatility traders expect over the next 30 days. The Cboe Nasdaq Volatility Index jumped more than 13 points to 38.3, its highest since April 11, 2025.

What set it off

The trigger, in the reporting, was political rather than economic. Democrats swept both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterms and won governorships in states including Texas, a major data centre hub, and investors read the result as a higher risk of tighter regulation for AI infrastructure. Selling concentrated where this year's gains were: the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index sank more than 11%, and options traders stayed bearish on chips into the close — puts accounted for $1.5 billion of the $1.7 billion in premium traded in the VanEck Semiconductor ETF, according to SpotGamma data cited in the reports. The fear reached Asia within hours: Taiwan's Taiex closed 4.51% lower on November 6, the Nikkei 225 fell 5.78%, and South Korea's Kospi briefly dropped more than 8%, triggering a trading halt. By Friday's US close the VIX had cooled to 25.64, still well above its long-run average of about 19.

What 19 past spikes show

Bespoke examined the 19 instances since 1990 in which the VIX rose at least five points from a starting level below 20. The median S&P 500 return was 4.2% three months later and 4.8% six months later, with gains 68% and 79% of the time respectively. The first month is the cautionary part of the same table: the average one-month return was negative 0.4%, dragged down by large declines after spikes in 1990 and on February 24, 2020, as the Covid selloff began. The same history was reported by CNBC and summarised by 24/7 Wall St. via Europe Says.

"These types of sharp spikes from placid levels are like a line of thunderstorms coming through in summer. The sky quickly darkens and wind gusts, but the loudest thunder and brightest lightning doesn't last long."

— Paul Hickey, co-founder, Bespoke Investment Group

Buffett's rule, and its limits

The episode revived Warren Buffett's most-cited line on market psychology, from his 1986 shareholder letter: "We simply attempt to be fearful when others are greedy and to be greedy only when others are fearful." The same passage limits the rule — Buffett wrote that he never tried to anticipate the arrival or departure of either mood and had no idea whether the market would go up, down or sideways in the near term. That is the honest frame for Bespoke's table: it is a description of 19 past episodes, not a forecast, and past performance does not guarantee future results.
